In this note, I share evidence of AI’s impact on growth, productivity, inflation, and labor, and I discuss the implications for markets and policy. * AI-linked investments, driven by a surge in demand, are lifting areas of investment growth in the US economy to a point where they’re contributing as much as consumer spending. * AI’s impact on US equity market earnings, profit margins, and performance has been substantial and well ahead of the economic impact, which is typical of a capital-intensive buildout. items.title: AI Trading Algorithms Can Make Markets Less Competitive
items.snippet: AI-driven trading can blunt competition and even lift prices in financial market...
items.raw_snippet: AI-driven trading can blunt competition and even lift prices in financial markets. * AI Trading algorithms (“Bots”) can set prices significantly higher than competitive levels. Artificial intelligence bots are increasingly acting as market makers, setting prices and matching buyers with sellers in financial markets. But they do not always make those markets more competitive. In practice, they don’t when it comes to AI. In practice, the AI would need far more data – potentially billions of trades – to learn to be more competitive, but financial markets move too quickly for that to happen. When that gap is smaller, it becomes easier and more profitable for bots to slightly undercut each other, which in theory should push prices down and make markets more competitive. In effect, they spread themselves too thin – the implication being the rules of the market can backfire when prices are set by algorithms. In the long run when more bots are added, prices move closer to the competitive “Glosten-Milgrom” benchmark.
